subject: Literature
title: Banned Newspapers and the Free Press
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Banned Newspapers and the Free Press.

hook.text: John Peter Zenger was jailed in 1734 for printing truthful articles criticizing the governor of New York.

buildup.text: Colonial law said that any criticism of government officials, even if true, counted as seditious libel.

discovery.text: His lawyer, Andrew Hamilton, argued that truth should be a defense against libel, a revolutionary legal concept.

twist.text: The jury acquitted Zenger, establishing the principle that truth cannot be censored, decades before the First Amendment.

climax.text: The Zenger case laid the foundation for press freedom that would be enshrined in the American Constitution.

punchline.text: One printer's trial created freedom of the press.

quiz.question: What legal precedent did the Zenger trial establish?
options: That newspapers must be licensed by the government
That truth is a defense against libel charges
That only government officials can publish news
